summaries.example: Imagine a school day. Recess is later than math class, and lunch is between them. We can describe these events by saying which came first. But we can also ask whether the present moment is special, whether yesterday still exists in some way, and whether tomorrow is already fixed. Philosophers use these questions to examine what time really is.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of time studies what time is, how events are ordered, and whether time genuinely passes. Some philosophers think time exists independently, like an empty container. Others think time is only made from relationships among events. They disagree about whether the future is already real, whether only the present exists, and whether objects have different “time slices” at different moments. The entry also discusses arguments about fatalism, time travel, the shape of time, physics, and how our ideas about time should guide our choices. It presents these as connected but unsettled questions rather than as one solved puzzle.
key_ideas: Philosophers ask whether time exists independently of events, or whether time is only the order and relations among events.
Some theories treat the present as especially real. Others say past, present, and future are all equally part of reality.
The A-theory uses past, present, and future as important features. The B-theory describes events as earlier or later than one another.
Philosophers also ask whether time can branch, loop, have a beginning, or contain more than one separate timeline.
Physics, especially ideas about relativity, influences debates about whether there is one objective present.
Questions about time affect how we think about choice, change, travel through time, and our concern for the future.
summaries.why_it_matters: Everyone plans, remembers, changes, and makes choices in time. Thinking carefully about time can show why the future may seem open, why the past feels different from the future, and why physics can challenge everyday ideas. It also helps us notice that a familiar experience—such as feeling time pass—is not automatically proof of what time is like in reality.

important_terms.definition: The view that everything that will happen is already unavoidable. Philosophers question whether this follows from the fact that future statements can be true or false.
A theory saying that only what is happening now exists. On this view, the past and future do not exist as present objects.
A theory saying that past, present, and future things all exist, even though they are located at different times.
A way of describing time by its ordering features, such as whether it has a beginning, an end, branches, or loops.
The idea that time really moves or passes, rather than merely containing events in an order.
The idea that time is more like a fourth direction, such as space, and does not literally flow.

questions_to_think_about: If tomorrow’s lunch is not decided yet, is the sentence “you will eat lunch tomorrow” true right now?
Does the past still exist, or does only the present exist?
Would time still exist if absolutely nothing changed?
Is time really moving, or does it only seem to move to people like us?
Would going to the past create a contradiction?

summaries.example: Suppose a leaf is green on September 7 and red on October 7. A B-theorist may say that all the relevant facts are tenseless: the leaf is green at one time and red at a later time. An A-theorist may say that this misses an important fact: one event is now past, another was once present, and another was future. The disagreement concerns whether tense and passage are features of reality or only ways creatures like us describe it.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of time examines the structure, reality, and significance of temporal order. Major disputes concern whether time is independent of events, whether it has a linear or more unusual topology, and whether future-directed claims are already true. McTaggart’s distinction between A-properties—past, present, and future—and B-relations—earlier and later—organizes the A-theory/B-theory debate. Related theories disagree about existence: presentism restricts existence to the present, eternalism includes all times, and the growing block includes the past and present. Further debates concern temporal parts, passage, time travel, relativity, entropy, quantum gravity, and rational concern for future selves. The entry emphasizes that these theories can be combined in different ways and that no single package follows automatically from one commitment.
key_ideas: The fatalist argument moves from claims about future truth to the conclusion that future events cannot be avoided. Critics challenge assumptions about propositions, truth values, and agency.
Reductionism or relationism treats time as nothing over and above temporal relations among events. Platonism or substantivalism treats time as independent of what happens in it.
McTaggart distinguished A-series ordering, involving past, present, and future, from B-series ordering, involving earlier and later. He argued that neither gives a satisfactory account of time.

Presentism, eternalism, and the growing block theory disagree about which temporally located objects exist. These views face different problems concerning talk about the past and future and the truth of historical or future claims.

Three-dimensionalism says an object is wholly present whenever it exists; four-dimensionalism explains persistence through temporal parts. This debate is linked to how changing properties are understood.

Special relativity challenges an objective present through the relativity of simultaneity, but the philosophical consequences depend partly on whether one treats the theory’s extra structure as indispensable.
summaries.why_it_matters: Time is tied to freedom, responsibility, identity, scientific explanation, and practical reasoning. A view about time can affect whether the future seems open, how persistence through change is understood, and whether concern for future people or future versions of oneself is rationally different from concern for present people. The subject also shows how ordinary experience, logic, metaphysics, and physics can support or pressure one another without settling every philosophical question.

important_terms.definition: The doctrine that whatever will happen is already unavoidable. A standard argument for it relies on future propositions being either true or false and on true predictions being unable to become false.
The principle that every proposition is either true or false. Rejecting this for some future contingent propositions supports an “open future” response to fatalism.
A position holding that time can be represented by a structure with features such as linearity, continuity, branching, loops, or a beginning and an end.
A family of views holding that important temporal facts involve being past, present, or future. These are called A-properties.
A family of views holding that temporal facts can be stated using earlier-than, later-than, and simultaneous-with relations, without an objective moving present.
The view that only present objects exist. Eternalism says past and future objects also exist; the growing block view says past and present objects exist but the future does not.
The view that an object extended through time has a distinct temporal part at each time, like a sequence of stages making up a whole.
The claim that time genuinely passes and is fundamentally unlike space. It is often associated with presentism, the A-theory, and three-dimensionalism, though the combinations are not mandatory.

questions_to_think_about: Does a true statement about a future event make that event unavoidable, or does the argument for fatalism assume too much about truth and agency?
Can a proposition change its truth value as time passes, or must truth be fixed once and for all?
Which view better explains ordinary talk about Socrates, dinosaurs, or future cities: presentism, eternalism, or the growing block theory?
Does the experience of temporal flow provide evidence for dynamic time, or could it result from perception and cognition?
If entropy explains the arrow of time, does that explain direction itself or merely track a direction already assumed?

summaries.example: Think about a group project due next week. You may feel that several outcomes are possible: the group might finish early, rush at the last minute, or miss the deadline. One philosopher might say that one of these outcomes is already fixed, even if you do not know which. Another might say that statements about such future choices are not yet true or false. A third might say that every time in the project’s history—planning, writing, and submission—exists as part of one larger timeline.
summaries.summary: Philosophy of time asks whether time is a thing in its own right, a network of relations, or a feature that emerges from change. It studies the shape of time and whether it must be linear, endless, continuous, or one single stream. Fatalism focuses on whether future events are unavoidable, while the open-future view questions whether every future statement is already true or false. The A-theory gives reality to past, present, and future; the B-theory explains time through earlier-later relations. These positions connect with presentism, eternalism, the growing block theory, and debates about temporal parts. The entry also links time to relativity, entropy, quantum physics, time travel, and rational decisions about the future.
key_ideas: Time may be independent of events, like a container, or may consist only of relations among events and things.
The future raises a puzzle about truth and freedom: knowing or stating what will happen does not obviously show that it must happen.
A-theorists regard past, present, and future as important features of reality; B-theorists think earlier and later relations are enough.
Presentism says only the present exists. Eternalism includes past and future, while the growing block includes the past and present but not the future.
The moving spotlight theory combines an eternal timeline with an objectively special present that changes location along it.
Time travel raises both scientific and philosophical questions, including whether backward causation or contradictions would result.
summaries.why_it_matters: Our ideas about time influence how we understand change, personal identity, freedom, and planning. They also reveal limits to common sense: physics may not support one universal present, and the feeling that time flows may arise from how minds process events. Studying competing theories encourages careful separation of what seems natural, what follows logically, and what science may support.

important_terms.definition: The view that future events cannot be prevented because they are already fixed or unavoidable. Philosophers examine whether this conclusion really follows from claims about future truth.
The idea that a statement must be either true or false. Some philosophers reject this for certain future events that are possible but not settled.
The structure used to represent time. It might be one straight line, a line with a beginning, a branching structure, or another arrangement.
A way of analyzing time using past, present, and future. These changing properties are called A-properties.
A way of analyzing time using fixed relations such as earlier than and later than. These are called B-relations.
The view that only present things exist. Its rivals include eternalism and the growing block theory.
The view that objects at different times have different temporal parts. An object can be understood as extended across time as well as space.
The view that events and objects are arranged in a complete structure and that time does not literally flow. It is often contrasted with the dynamic theory.

questions_to_think_about: Is a future choice free if a true statement about it already exists?
Would time be possible if the universe contained no change at all?
Does describing an object as green at one time and red at another fully explain change?
Could a timeline branch or loop without becoming logically impossible?
Should the way time feels to us count as evidence about what time is really like?
